title: Lesson 51: Agent Identity: OAuth, Service Accounts, and Scoped Permissions
description: An agent is a machine actor, and a machine actor needs a machine identity: credentials it can present to an API, a scope limited to the least it needs to do, and a way to be rotated and revoked when it is no longer trusted. The authorization code grant lets an agent act on a specific user's behalf without ever seeing the user's password, while the client credentials grant lets it act on its own behalf using its own credentials. A service account gives a long-running agent a durable non-human identity with its own permissions, and OAuth scopes express least privilege by limiting what a token may do.

questions.question: An agent needs to read a specific user's tickets so it can answer that user's support questions. Which OAuth flow should it use, and why?
options: The client credentials grant, because the agent authenticates with its own credentials and needs no user involvement
The authorization code grant, because the user authenticates and approves the access, and the agent never sees the user's password
The resource owner password grant, because the agent needs the user's password to act reliably
The implicit grant, because it issues an access token directly without any user interaction
questions.explanation: The lesson says the authorization code grant answers how an agent acts on behalf of a specific user: the user authenticates with the authorization server and approves the access, and the user's password never reaches the agent. The client credentials grant is for the agent acting on its own behalf with no user in the loop.

questions.question: Why should a long-running agent that does scheduled work use a service account rather than a human's account?
options: A service account is a non-human identity with its own credentials and permissions, so the agent's actions are not attributed to a person and can be scoped and revoked independently
A service account inherits all the permissions of the person who created it, which is simpler to manage
A service account never needs its credentials rotated, so it is more convenient
A service account is required only for agents that act on behalf of users, not for scheduled workloads
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that a service account is a special kind of account representing a non-human actor, with its own credentials and permissions, distinct from every person. Because it is not tied to a person, it does not carry a human's permissions and can be granted, scoped, rotated, and revoked independently.

questions.question: An agent's service account credentials leak. What limits the damage an attacker can do with them?
options: The agent's system prompt, which instructs it to refuse harmful requests
The OAuth scopes granted to the token, which limit what the token may do on the resource server
The agent's model provider, which filters unauthorized API calls
The user's password, which the attacker would also need to act
questions.explanation: The lesson says scopes are the mechanism for least privilege: the token the agent receives is limited to the scopes it was granted, and the resource server enforces those scopes on every request. The smaller the scope, the smaller the blast radius when credentials leak.
